items.title: FRAME-PS: a typology-specific method for assessing climate resilience in urban public spaces
items.summary_raw: FRAME-PS (Field-ready Resilience Assessment Model for Public Spaces) is developed as a transparent, repeatable, and typology-specific model for assessing public space resilience across problem domains. The article operationalizes its climate resilience module, since climate-related stressors cut across spatial, ecological, social, economic, and governance dimensions and directly affect everyday public space performance. The module follows four stages: assembling spatial criteria, eliciting typology-specific expert weights, translating criteria into a standardized field assessment protocol, and aggregating site scores into a Composite Resilience Score (CRS). For the square typology, it uses 24 climate resilience criteria to connect criterion importance with on-site performance. A pilot application at Istanbul's Taksim Square demonstrates the module at field scale, without claiming generalization to all squares. The assessment produced a CRS of 1.71 out of 5.00, corresponding to 34.2% of the maximum score. Deficits clustered in high-weight, low-score criteria, including climatic shelter, tree canopy, pervious surfaces, material performance, water features, and nature-based cooling. The weight × score logic identifies intervention priorities along exposed desire lines and waiting areas. FRAME-PS provides a practical decision aid, while future multi-site and multi-season applications should test transferability and recalibrate scoring anchors.

items.title: Soil Carbon Sequestration Potential of Climate-Smart Agronomic Practices: A Critical Review
items.source_name: Journal of Advances in Biology & Biotechnology
items.summary_raw: Agricultural soils can contribute to climate mitigation through management that increases organic carbon inputs, limits avoidable losses and sustains favourable conditions for carbon retention. Yet higher soil carbon concentrations, larger stocks relative to conventional management and additional atmospheric carbon removal are not interchangeable outcomes. This critical narrative review evaluates the sequestration potential of cover cropping, diversified rotations, residue retention, reduced tillage, organic amendments, biochar, balanced nutrient management, water management and agroforestry in predominantly mineral agricultural soils. Verified scholarly literature with publication coverage through 30 July 2026 was synthesised according to intervention mechanisms, measurement validity, temporal persistence and whole-system greenhouse gas consequences. The most consistent evidence supports maintaining or increasing plant-derived inputs and combining compatible practices, rather than assuming that disturbance reduction alone produces substantial whole-profile gains. Cover crops commonly increase topsoil carbon, but responses depend on biomass production, growing windows, water availability and nitrogen management. Imported amendments can enlarge receiving-soil stocks without demonstrating equivalent additional removal at landscape scale. Biochar offers a distinct persistence pathway, conditional on feedstock sourcing, production emissions and realistic decay accounting…

items.title: Monthly Magazine
items.summary_raw: How is the structure of electricity production in Poland changing? What emissions are involved? How are raw material prices evolving? Here is a summary of the most important data from the electricity industry. Updated monthly.

items.title: Visual metaphors, cartoons and science communication
items.source_name: Journal of Language and Pop Culture
items.summary_raw: Abstract This study highlights the semiotic and textual mechanisms underlying the use of visual metaphors in cartoons aimed at scientific dissemination and debate. Visual metaphors are indeed a powerful tool for disseminating knowledge, and in cartoons or comics they can prove a very effective strategy; however, the possibility of using metaphors to frame reality, thus influencing public opinion, is an aspect that must be taken into consideration. This appears to be particularly interesting when scientific concepts are communicated to a large audience. To address this issue, the present contribution analyses the role of cartoons ( dessins de presse ) in a corpus of French-language publications (books and cartoons collections) about the COVID-19 pandemic and climate change, to investigate what happens when visual metaphors are used to popularise complex scientific concepts in social debate, and the risks of simplification or polarisation these kinds of metaphors can generate. It describes different kinds of conceptual metaphors involved in the data, their visual realisations and the relationship between the topic (COVID-19, climate change), the nature of the metaphorical conceptual interaction (creative or conventional metaphors) and visual metaphorical models. It thus highlights the potential effects of visual metaphors on the readers’ perception.

items.title: Breaking the car-dependence trap: Policy mixes, structural constraints, and sustainable mobility performance across Italian provinces
items.summary_raw: Breaking car dependence is a key challenge for achieving sustainable urban mobility, but the adoption and effectiveness of policy frameworks to reduce reliance on private cars vary substantially across territories. This study examines these territorial differences across Italian provinces by combining socio-economic, institutional, environmental, and mobility indicators in a multi-stage empirical design. Specifically, propensity score matching is used to compare provinces that adopt a comprehensive sustainable mobility policy mix with otherwise similar provinces that adopt a narrower set of policy measures. Subsequently, data envelopment analysis assesses how efficiently provinces transform public transport, fleet quality, and mobility resources into sustainable mobility outcomes, specifically public transport demand and shared mobility availability. Finally, fractional logit and logistic models examine, respectively, the factors associated with efficiency and policy adoption. The results show that provinces adopting a broader policy mix display higher mobility efficiency scores. At the same time, car dependence emerges as a structural constraint and is associated with both lower mobility efficiency and a reduced likelihood of adopting such a policy mix. This cross-sectional study contributes to the literature by linking policy adoption, mobility-system efficiency, and structural car dependence within a single empirical framework. The findings suggest that effective…

items.title: “Geothermal resources for energy transition?” – Understanding Northern Canadian residents' perspectives on geothermal developments in their communities
Renewable Energy-Based Microgrids for Rural Electrification in Nigeria: Opportunities and Challenges
items.source_name: ABUAD Journal of Engineering Research and Development (AJERD)
items.summary_raw: Rural electrification is still one of the most serious and intractable development issues facing Nigeria, a country with a rich source of renewable energy sources and a high rate of energy access gap in the world. About 86 million Nigerians, who mostly dwell in rural and peri-urban settings, in the North-East and the North-West geopolitical zones lack access to dependable electricity, which continues to ensure poverty, limit agricultural output, weaken the focus on healthcare services, and slows the pace of industrial progress. Microgrids based on renewable energy that combine solar photovoltaic (PV), wind, small hydro, biogas, and battery energy storage technologies into geographically distributed, autonomous power systems locally have become the technically viable and economically competitive modality of providing reliable electricity to the geographically remote rural populations that cannot be served by conventional grid extension. The paper is a detailed scholarly review article of the prospects and challenges of the implementation of microgrids on renewable energy to electrify rural Nigerians. The endowment of renewable resources in the country is monitored in a systematic manner; the major potentials of the country include high solar irradiation (4.2-6.2 kWh/m2/day), high wind potential in the north of Nigeria, large agricultural biomass residues, and new opportunities of policy and regulations. At the same time, the main threats, such as disjointed regulatory…

items.title: Democratizing expertise: lived experience as evidence in citizens’ assemblies
items.summary_raw: Democratic policymaking is said to require the wisdom of crowds. Yet complex issues require expert input. Citizens’ assemblies, which bring together randomly selected citizens and professional experts, appear to reconcile these demands. However, professional experts often exert strong influence on assembly members, risking the marginalization of lay and local knowledge. This paper evaluates an intervention in the Southampton Citizens’ Climate Assembly that introduced ‘citizen witnesses’ – individuals sharing lived experience relevant to the topic with the assembly members – to foster a more inclusive and democratic knowledge-building process. Analyzing survey data, field notes, and interviews with assembly members, we find that citizen witnesses complemented professional expertise and influenced the assembly not only by providing additional information but also by reshaping how assembly members understood the issue under deliberation. Their testimonies prompted reflection on blind spots, privilege and unequal exposure to policy consequences, broadening assembly members’ understanding of the policy problem. They also encouraged members to draw more confidently on their own experiences during deliberation, reinforcing the legitimacy of lived experience as a source of knowledge in collective decision-making. These findings suggest that citizen witnesses can help democratize expertise within citizens’ assemblies by elevating the standing of lay knowledge alongside professional…

items.title: Pakistan's solar boom: Visible and invisible grid defection in a high-cost, low-reliability power system
items.summary_raw: Between 2019 and 2025, solar generation on Pakistan's grid grew fourteen-fold, from 2.6 TWh to 36.6 TWh, reaching 22.5% of grid output and peaking at roughly one-third of monthly generation. Ember data through March 2026 show the boom continuing: solar supplied 32.3% of total generation in the first quarter of 2026 (12.1 of 37.5 TWh), overtaking coal, gas, nuclear and hydropower to become the single largest source on the system. This paper assembles regulatory, trade and generation data to explain why one of the world's fastest solar transitions occurred in a fiscally distressed power system, and to characterise who is leaving the grid and how. We document two distinct solar booms. The first is a metered, net-metering boom (6.1 GW and over 378,000 consumers by June 2025), concentrated overwhelmingly, with roughly 85% of capacity, in the six best-performing distribution jurisdictions, and driven by tariffs that more than doubled in three years. The second is a largely invisible, off-grid and behind-the-meter boom, revealed by the gap between roughly 40 GW of cumulative panel imports since FY2020 and the much smaller registered capacity, and concentrated where service failure is severest: utilities whose monitored load shedding exceeds 8–10 h per day, transmission and distribution losses approach 40%, and recovery falls to 39%. Using NEPRA's FY2024–25 performance evaluation data, the study shows that formal grid defection tracks affordability stress in well-served…

items.title: Prioritizing decarbonization technologies for climate-neutral railway systems: A qualitative technology assessment of Korea’s rail sector
items.summary_raw: Railways are widely recognized as a low-carbon transport mode, but achieving climate-neutral railway systems requires a broader transition beyond modal shift, spanning propulsion technologies, energy supply, infrastructure management, digital operation, and climate resilience. This study develops a document-informed, interpretive technology assessment framework to examine railway decarbonization technologies, using Korea as a case study. Global technology and policy agendas were reviewed and classified into four domains—low-carbon propulsion and electrification, energy optimization and renewable integration, digital and AI-based operation, and climate-resilient infrastructure—and assessed against environmental relevance, technological maturity, operational applicability, policy/regulatory readiness, and R&D urgency. Korea has relatively mature conventional railway technologies, but significant gaps remain in hydrogen and battery-based propulsion, renewable energy–rail integration, standards and certification, and decarbonization-specific demonstration infrastructure. The assessment identifies distinct implementation conditions and R&D priorities across the four domains. Regenerative braking, energy storage systems, energy management systems, and AI-based operation optimization are classified as near-term priorities because of their relatively high operational applicability and potential for integration into existing railway systems. Renewable energy–rail integration…

items.title: Travelling as a Cultural Activity: Framing Perceptions of Communication in Balkan Travel Vlogs
items.summary_raw: This study examines travel vlogs as a cultural activity. It aims to determine how viewers interpret the narrative structure that the content creator establishes in travel vlogs. In this context, the video titled “Does It Make Sense to Visit the Balkan Countries on a Tour? What Are the Extra Costs? (We Visited 5 Countries in 7 Days Without a Visa)”, published on the YouTube channel Sonsuz Keşif, which was selected through purposive sampling, was analysed. The data obtained from the video were analysed using the MAXQDA programme. The video content was analysed using Fairclough’s discourse analysis approach, whilst the viewer comments posted beneath the video were analysed using content analysis. In this mixed-methods study, two main themes and 12 sub-themes were identified across viewer comments and video content. The study found that the video content covered historical and cultural information, cultural identity, food and drink, encouragement to travel, shopping budgets, and local beliefs. Viewer comments, meanwhile, focused on routes and guidance, aesthetics and viewing, budget, safety, culture and identity, and comfort and luxury. In conclusion, this research shows that while vloggers give cultural and affective meaning to their travels through the content they produce, viewers translate that meaning into practical questions for their own travel plans. This suggests that viewers actively consume vlog content and rework it to meet their travel-planning needs.

items.title: State‐Initiated Climate Intermediaries Shaping Climate Governance–Needed Facilitators of Dialogue for Societal Transition to Net Zero?
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT As governments intensify efforts to achieve net zero goals, they increasingly rely on forms of indirect governance to mobilise societal actors and facilitate climate action. Governance literature focuses on orchestration by organisations and governments that engage intermediaries to pursue shared governance goals. While intermediaries are recognised in climate governance as go‐between organisations operating between governance levels to affect climate policy, less is known about states that establish and design intermediaries for steering climate action. This paper unpacks policy characteristics of what we call state‐initiated climate intermediaries (SICI) to gain a nuanced understanding of this dynamic. It examines cases of SICIs in Sweden and the Netherlands using grey literature analysis. Case analysis is guided by a novel conceptual framework that bridges orchestration theory with mission‐oriented innovation policy. The analysis indicates that mission‐oriented policy of SICIs that encourages cross‐sectoral participation and dialogue with the wider public facilitates inclusive climate action. However, neither intermediary provides systematic mechanisms for tracking participants' implementation of voluntary commitments. The available evidence therefore indicates facilitation and stakeholder mobilisation, but does not permit conclusions about the resulting climate outcomes. This paper makes a conceptual contribution to climate governance literature by defining…

items.title: Towards Common Ground: Perspectives on Energy Transitions in Canadian Oil and Gas Producing Municipalities
items.summary_raw: Abstract Oil and gas producing municipalities host Canada's highest‐emitting industries while facing economic and social risks as the country pursues carbon neutrality. Understanding how these communities envision their economic futures, and the barriers and enablers they encounter in pursuing low‐carbon opportunities, can inform decision‐makers seeking both emissions reductions and more resilient local economies. This study engages ten municipal economic development staff in British Columbia and Alberta to capture their perspectives on transition pathways. Findings demonstrate that staff are exploring diversification but face substantial barriers, including limited staff, technical, and fiscal capacity and the absence of a coherent transition vision. Addressing these challenges requires governance transformation. We argue that transition strategies must move beyond top‐down, universal mandates and embrace more locally grounded approaches. Community‐supported, place‐relevant visions for low‐carbon transitions, co‐created with municipal actors, must be supported by integrated policy packages built on whole‐systems modalities rather than narrow green jobs or sectoral focuses.

items.title: Jochen Flasbarth appointed as next CEO of the European Climate Foundation
items.summary_raw: 6 October 2026 | The Supervisory Board has appointed Jochen Flasbarth as the European Climate Foundation’s next Chief Executive Officer. Jochen has accepted the role, and the necessary arrangements relating to his transition from German public service are now being…

items.title: Parental responses to climate threat: Italian Validation of the Climate Self-Protection Scale and the role of eco-defenses, epistemic stances, and eco-anxiety
items.summary_raw: Climate change has psychological repercussions that challenge individuals’ basic assumptions about stability and safety and contribute to emotional suffering. Parents may be particularly vulnerable to eco-anxiety, given concerns about the long-term impact on their children’s well-being. This research, conducted in Italy, examined how defenses against climate change (“eco-defenses”) and epistemic stances (trust, mistrust, credulity) shape parents’ eco-anxiety across two studies. In Study 1 ( N = 1,259 Italian-speaking adults), we validated the Italian version of the Climate Self-Protection Scale, confirming its original five-factor structure: Rationalization, Avoidance, Denial of Personal Outcome Severity, Denial of Global Outcome Severity, and Denial of Guilt. In Study 2 ( N = 986 Italian parents), we investigated how eco-defenses and epistemic stances, and their interaction, were associated with the four eco-anxiety symptoms: affective symptoms, rumination, behavioral symptoms, and anxiety about personal impact. Both eco-defenses and epistemic stances showed significant associations with eco-anxiety, highlighting distinct pathways through which parents regulate the emotional burden of, and process information about, climate change. These findings identify eco-defenses and epistemic stances as key psychological processes in parental adaptation to ecological threats and highlight potential intervention targets to support family resilience.

items.title: Legitimations of Consumer Purchases in Charitable Media: A Critical Discourse Analysis of Fundraising Appeals for Clean Water
items.summary_raw: Since the 1980s, companies and nonprofit organizations (NPOs) have used cause-related marketing (CRM) to generate donations for causes by selling products and services. This study examines the CRM campaigns (N = 177) for clean water projects, focusing on how companies and NPOs frame experiences of human suffering and consumer purchases as purposeful actions. It proposes CRM campaigns are “charitable media texts” with distinct ways of issue framing, driving issue attention, and forming coalitions. The analysis showed that water insecurity was narrated using three perspectives: political-economic, cultural, and environmental, forming coalitions around climate change, human rights, and gender inequality. Representations of companies, NPOs, and individuals diverged in their uptake of responsibility as an obligation and accountability, but portrayals of the government’s role were under-represented. Moral and cautionary narratives drew attention to water insecurity using persuasion and ideational coercion, shifting the responsibility for helping water-insecure communities from an institutional obligation to individual responsibility.

items.title: Social and labour policies can unlock the climate deadlock
items.summary_raw: Every five years, signatory countries to the Paris Agreement update their Nationally Determined Contributions, outlining national climate policies and greenhouse gas (GHG) emission targets. We propose a simulation modelling framework leveraging data from the system of national accounts, national GHG emission inventories, and household and labour force surveys. With supply-and-use tables at its core, the framework assesses how structural changes in economies, driven by climate policies such as the adoption of low-emission energy technologies, affect direct, indirect, and induced employment by industry. We apply this approach to seven economically diverse countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, examining policies related to renewable energy, industrial processes, sustainable agriculture and tourism. Estimates of technological change are informed by national statistical data, expert knowledge and secondary literature. We find that climate policies generally lead to net-positive nationwide employment gains. The findings can support governments in designing complementary Just Transition policies that maximise gains and improve fairness.Highlights – We analyse ‘what-if’ NDC climate policies using country-specific inter-industry trajectory models for seven different Sub-Saharan African countries.– We find that most climate policies yield net-positive nationwide employment gains.– However, job losses occur in carbon-intensive sectors, with industry-level impacts depending on the nature of…

items.title: How digital literacy and digital entrepreneurship education shape digital entrepreneurial intention among agriculture students
items.summary_raw: Digital entrepreneurship has become an important driver of innovation and economic development, yet the mechanisms linking digital competencies and educational experiences to digital entrepreneurial intention (DEI) remain insufficiently understood in agricultural higher education. Extending the Theory of Planned Behavior, this study examines how digital literacy and digital entrepreneurship education relate to DEI through attitudes and perceived behavioral control. Data were collected from 300 agriculture students at two Iranian public universities and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that digital literacy was not directly associated with DEI but was positively associated with digital entrepreneurship education. Digital entrepreneurship education, in turn, showed positive direct and indirect associations with DEI through attitudes and perceived behavioral control. Subjective norms were not significantly associated with DEI. These findings suggest that students’ digital entrepreneurial intentions may be shaped more strongly by perceived desirability and feasibility than by perceived social pressure. The study extends the TPB by positioning digital literacy and digital entrepreneurship education as antecedents of DEI and highlighting attitudes and perceived behavioral control as key proximal mechanisms. For agricultural higher education, the findings underscore the value of integrating foundational digital skills…

items.title: N-LAS-IAM: Climate change in a balance-of-payments framework
items.summary_raw: Climate change is becoming a macro-financial development problem for peripheral economies, yet integrated assessment models remain poorly equipped to analyse climate vulnerability in externally constrained developing countries. Existing heterodox models are mostly closed or global, while balance-of-payments-constrained growth models treat climate in reduced form and incompletely formalise the financial channel. This paper introduces the N-LAS-IAM, a recursive framework coupling a Thirlwall–Hussain growth core with endogenous green structural change, capital flows under financial fragility, sovereign risk, and a climate module mapping global emissions into damages that feed back into profitability and sovereign fragility. Green structural change is endogenised through logistic diffusion equations governing trade income elasticities as functions of green R&D and the real exchange rate. The model is explored via Monte Carlo experiments in which damage intensity and climate-to-risk transmission vary while emissions, policy, and structural-change parameters remain fixed. Three results emerge. First, higher damage produces a more fragile debt regime with elevated spreads, tighter financing, and prolonged deleveraging. Second, damages widen the elasticity gap between exports and imports, slowing green upgrading and locking the economy into lower-sophistication trade patterns. Third, the damage-to-fragility relationship is nonlinear: below a threshold the economy absorbs shocks, but…

items.title: Is it (socially) contagious? Capturing spatial-temporal trends of pro-environmental gardening using hazard models
items.summary_raw: Planting native gardens on verges, a form of underutilised public land, can provide biodiversity-enhancing and water-saving benefits that help achieve urban environmental goals. As a result, many governments in Australia offer support programs to encourage the adoption of native vegetation gardens on verges, yet there is limited data on actual adoption rates. By conducting a physical audit of two case study sites within the Perth capital region of Western Australia, we identify verge garden adoption rates of 11% in the Town of Claremont and 18% in the suburb of Daglish. We estimate a hazard model to examine relationships between neighbours' verge garden adoption decisions. Duration analysis shows that a household's adoption of a verge garden may positively impact their neighbours' future decisions, suggesting contagion and social mimicry effects. Between having no other verge garden conversions and the maximum level of Influence, we find a 4- to 44-fold increase in the probability of adopting a verge garden in Daglish and Claremont, respectively. We also conduct a survey of verge garden adopters to better understand the drivers of adoption, which reinforces the importance of neighbourhood norms in motivating adoption decisions. Large proportions (87% in Claremont and 39% in Daglish) of verge conversions were undertaken without participation in any government support programs. Our results suggest that local governments may achieve higher rates of behaviour change under…

items.title: Beyond the Green Lung: Relational Plant Ethics in the Climate Crisis
items.summary_raw: As climate change victims, plants are gaining attention. However, their value has been characterized as carbon sinks, food sources, or planetary lungs. The study proposes a relational plant ethics that goes beyond utilitarian calculations without ignoring plant science. Based on recent plant neurobiology, environmental virtue ethics, and nature aesthetics, I propose that plants deserve moral consideration not only because they satisfy human interests but also because they organize, collaborate, and thrive, challenging anthropocentric beliefs about intelligent life. The paper argues that plant intelligence challenges the ontological distinction between subjects and objects, that flourishing provides a justifiable basis for attributing the good-of-itself to vegetal life without biocentric egalitarianism, and that empathetic relationships with plants, such as repair and healing, are self-care for humans in an ecological crisis. I argue that plant ethics can offer new conservation arguments and a critical lens to evaluate capitalist climate change temporalities.

items.title: Modelling the decision making in light of the energy transformation in Poland: nuclear plant construction case study
items.source_name: Innovation The European Journal of Social Science Research
items.summary_raw: This article examines decision-making in Poland’s nuclear energy programme within the broader green transformation. Applying a rational actor decision model, it analyses the interaction of three variables – public support, intragovernmental unity, and external pressure – across successive governments from 2015 to 2025. The study identifies three distinct phases of policy development shaped by shifts in these factors. Decisive actions, including site selection and international agreements, occurred only when public opinion, political cohesion, and external pressures converged, while their absence led to delay or inertia. Empirical evidence is drawn from public opinion data, party manifestos, parliamentary debates, and external drivers such as EU climate regulations and geopolitical disruptions following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The findings confirm that alignment of the three variables accelerates decision-making, whereas misalignment produces stagnation. The article contributes to research on energy policy and political decision-making by offering an empirically grounded theoretical model explaining variation in Poland’s nuclear policy outcomes.

items.title: Changing Urban Forest Cover and Climate Variability in Bamenda, Cameroon: A Spatio-temporal Assessment
items.source_name: International Journal of Environment and Climate Change
items.summary_raw: This paper examines how urban forest change and climate variability jointly shape hazard exposure in Bamenda. Using a mixed-methods design, it combines Landsat classification (1984, 2004, 2025), a 75-year rainfall series (1951-2025), a temperature window (1984-2023), a 400-household survey, key-informant interviews and field observation, organised within an analytical framework where regional climate provides the trigger, urban forest and built form modify exposure, and household capacity conditions sensitivity. City-wide forest fell from 11,170.8 ha in 1984 to 10,856.3 ha in 2025 (-2.8%), but municipal trajectories diverged: Bamenda I lost 38.8%, and Bamenda III lost 22.3%, while Bamenda II gained 51.6%. Mean monthly rainfall intensity declined from 213.4 mm (1951-1970) to 139.4 mm (2011-2025), with a highly significant trend of -1.17 mm yr⁻¹ (R²=0.581; p=2.04×10⁻¹⁵). Mean temperature rose from 18.56°C (1984-1990) to 22.97°C (2013-2023). Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) shifted from wet extremes in the 1950s-1960s to severe-to-extreme drought after 2007, including 2016 (SPI=-2.49) and a six-year severe-drought run from 2020 to 2025. Visual analytics, including graphs, heat maps, box plots, scatter plots, correlation matrices and spider charts, make co-movements visible. Flooding in Mulang, Ndamukong, Ngomgham and Ntarinkon and slope instability in Abangoh, Sisia and Mbatu are interpreted as joint outcomes of a drier, more variable climate and fragmented forest. Forest…

items.title: Analysis of Nigerian Newspapers' Portrayal of Climate Change Effects on Food Security
items.source_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGLISH LANGUAGE AND COMMUNICATION STUDIES
items.summary_raw: This study explored how Nigerian newspapers—The Guardian and Daily Trust—report climate change and its impact on food security, using framing theory as a guide. It specifically examined the patterns of story types, use of different frames and representation of voices in the newspapers. A content analysis of 394 articles revealed that feature articles were predominant, with limited presence of editorials and interviews. Findings also revealed that economic factors were the most dominant frame on climate change reports. It was also found that government officials were the most frequently mentioned sources of information, while farmers, women, youth, and scientists were given little attention. Thus, the narrative about climate change tends to be less inclusive and supportive of internal stakeholder participation. The paper concludes that climate issues were given moderate attention by Nigerian newspapers, which can only influence the public’s knowledge about climate-related food shortages to some extent. This highlights the need for a wider range of stories and reliable information, along with more responsible reporting, for national stability and sustainable system for food security.

items.title: Climate change education for children: a critical integrative review and the participation–emotion–resilience (PER) framework
items.summary_raw: Climate change education (CCE) in early childhood and primary settings has expanded rapidly, yet remains unevenly theorised with respect to children’s participation, emotional experiences, and resilience. While existing approaches frequently emphasise knowledge acquisition, pro-environmental behaviour, or coping skills, they offer limited explanatory insight into why children’s engagement with climate issues can simultaneously create agency, anxiety, hope, or disengagement. This critical integrative review synthesises 47 empirical, conceptual, review, and policy-oriented studies to examine how participation, emotion, and resilience are conceptualised and enacted in CCE for young children. Drawing on established guidance for integrative synthesis, the review identifies three patterned tendencies across the literature: constrained forms of participation that prioritise expression over influence; heightened attention to climate emotions without corresponding structural responsiveness; and resilience framings that risk individualisation in the absence of collective and rights-based supports. To explain these patterns, the review advances the Participation–Emotion–Resilience (PER) framework, which conceptualises participation, emotion, and resilience as mutually constitutive processes rather than discrete domains. Grounded in children’s rights research and aligned with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, the PER framework elucidates how the quality of participatory…

items.title: The Uncanny Anthropocene: Myth, Animals and Climate Anxiety in Amitav Ghosh's Gun Island
items.source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.summary_raw: This article examines Amitav Ghosh’s Gun Island (2019) as a literary response to the cultural condition of the Anthropocene, arguing that the novel stages climate change as an experience of the uncanny: the return of what modern rationality had repressed, in the form of myth, animal agency and bodily dread. Drawing on Freud’s account of the unheimlich, postcolonial ecocriticism and recent research on climate anxiety, the study shows how the legend of the Gun Merchant, the anomalous behaviour of snakes, spiders and dolphins, and the despairing journeys of migrants together unsettle the boundary between the familiar and the strange, the human and the nonhuman, the past and the present. The article contends that Ghosh converts climate anxiety from a private affect into a shared narrative problem, and that the novel’s mythic structure offers a provisional, if unsettled, way of imagining planetary dwelling.

items.title: Qualitative Study on Strengthening Universal Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics Education: An Exploration of SUSTAIN-STEM Model
items.source_name: Federal University Gusau Faculty of Education Journal
items.summary_raw: Despite global commitments to the 2030 Agenda, STEM education remains largely disconnected from pressing sustainability challenges such as climate change, energy, and waste. This conceptual paper argues that integrating sustainability is critical to strengthening universal STEM education that is equitable, relevant, and impact-driven. Drawing on the UNESCO ESD framework and Systems Thinking, the paper proposes the SUSTAIN-STEM Model: a 7-dimension framework comprising Systems Thinking, Use of Local Context, Sustainable Innovation, Teacher Capacity, Assessment for Impact, Inclusivity, and Networking. The model repositions STEM from mere content delivery to solving real-world sustainability problems through green pedagogy, community-based projects, and inclusive practices. Implications are discussed for curriculum redesign, teacher education in Colleges of Education, Policy Support, and low-cost green labs. Key challenges including resource constraints and exam-focused cultures are addressed with strategies such as partnerships and open educational resources. The paper concludes that Universal STEM education must evolve into STEM for sustainable development to achieve SDG 4 and SDG 13.

items.title: Julia Bläsius to lead Agora Industry Germany
Exploring the Role of Traditional Knowledge in Climate Change Adaptation among Rural Communities in Kogi State: Implications for Climate Communication and Policy
items.source_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGLISH LANGUAGE AND COMMUNICATION STUDIES
items.summary_raw: The environmental and economic difficulties arising from climate change affect developing world rural populations with increasing intensity. Traditional knowledge serves as the main focus for understanding climate change adaptation processes in Kogi State’s rural populace while contributing to policy frameworks and climate messaging strategies. The study examines how traditional knowledge supports rural communities during climate change adaptation and it examines the performance of communication methods for weaving indigenous understanding into official adaptation procedures. The study employed surveys as well as interviews and focus group discussions to obtain data from 255 participants in nine rural communities of Kogi State. The analysis focused on 246 responses collected during this research. It showed traditional adaptation techniques used by local communities extensively since they exist as integrated parts of their cultural practices. The research demonstrated that traditional community communication practices of storytelling and communal meetings alongside folklore serve as essential forces behind both climate awareness growth and community engagement development. The gap between traditional knowledge and national climate policy frameworks remains large because there is inadequate documentation and inadequate involvement of traditional leaders. Through the application of the Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) Theory, the study validated indigenous climate governance…

items.title: Tell Me Your Story: The Narratives of Sexual Assault Survivors on One College Campus
items.summary_raw: Approximately 20% of college students will be sexually assaulted during their university years, leading to prolonged physical and emotional repercussions. Out of fear, rebuke, and dismissal, most survivors choose not to report the attack. Those who do report often experience unsatisfactory outcomes. The cultural climate of college life, coupled with gendered scripts ingrained before campus enrollment, contributes to environments that conflate sex and power, dismiss consent, and allow campus complicity. To help break the silence, we collected the stories of 129 sexual assault survivors at one small state college in the Southeastern United States. Using basic demographic information and qualitative analysis, four themes emerged across narratives. Threaded throughout each theme’s description are direct quotes from survivors, boldly telling their stories. Study findings highlight survivors’ experiences centered on ambiguity and trust violations, ongoing impact, social and institutional betrayals, and suggestions from survivors. Lastly, survivors provide firsthand suggestions for making campuses more just, safe, and responsive.

items.title: Máme terminál i strategii. Moravskoslezský kraj láká na své území velké investory
items.summary_raw: Skladovou plochu přes 120 tisíc metrů čtverečních a více než 750 nových pracovních míst nabízí první automotive logistické centrum společnosti DP World v Česku. To letos v létě zahájilo svůj provoz v Ostrava Airport Multimodal Parku v Mošnově a...

items.title: Rivian Rolls to a New Record Quarter
items.summary_raw: The past three months have been crucial for Rivian, America’s biggest all-electric car company not run by Elon Musk. The California-based automaker debuted the R2, its long-awaited and somewhat more affordable sport utility vehicle. (Our reviewer gave it high marks .) Rivian also formally took out a nearly $6.6 billion loan from the Department of Energy to finance its new Georgia factory. And it finally unveiled the plans for that facility, which will include a rail tie-in and a 1,000-acre preserved woodland. All that was well and good, but the crucial question remained: How is the R2 selling? And the answer is: Pretty well, seemingly! Rivian delivered 19,248 vehicles last quarter, beating analyst expectations and setting a new all-time quarterly sales record. More importantly, its vehicle deliveries have now recovered above where they stood in the third quarter of last year — a key milestone, since President Trump and Congress ended the federal government’s consumer-side EV incentives last September. Tesla is seemingly also about to clear that threshold, although nobody outside the firm knows for sure. Elon Musk’s company doesn’t break out its sales by continent or model, but it delivered 486,532 vehicles last year — just about 2% below last year’s third quarter results. items.title: What a President Can and Can’t Do Under the Senate Permitting Bill
items.summary_raw: O ne of the non-negotiables for Senate Democrats in putting together a bipartisan permitting bill was to limit the president’s ability to reverse federal project approvals or otherwise gum up the works for developments they simply dislike. The authors’ goal was to prevent a situation like the one we’re in now, where Trump has revoked permits for wind farms, refused to permit new ones, and tried to stop construction of fully permitted offshore wind projects. But the language on “project certainty” in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is technology neutral — it would protect fossil fuels as much as clean energy. While Trump has perhaps gone the furthest of any president in using the authorities of the executive branch to enact his preferences, his Democratic predecessors have taken similar steps to stop mines, pipelines, and oil and gas drilling — often in the name of stopping climate change. “This bill is clearly looking backwards at five to 10 years of case studies in how an executive branch can delay or revoke permits, and it is targeted at those case studies,” Travis Annatoyn, an attorney at the law firm Arnold & Porter and the former deputy solicitor for energy and mineral resources at the Interior Department under Biden, told me. The bill section in question contains two key provisions. The first would make it illegal for a federal agency to rescind, terminate, or alter a federal authorization or permit, or to prevent the construction or operation of a…

items.title: Ancient DNA challenges to admixture narratives: Insights from Notre-Dame Cemetery (1683–1796) in Colonial Montreal, Canada
items.summary_raw: Historical narratives of early colonization in Quebec frequently portray French–Indigenous relations as cooperative and characterized by admixture; which are often mobilized in modern debates on false-indigeneity. These narratives have been studied through genealogical, genetic, and bioarchaeological analyses, yet individuals of African descent remain mostly absent from them, while Indigenous peoples are framed largely in relation to colonists. Notre-Dame Cemetery (1683–1796) in Tiohtià:ke-Montréal offers a unique window onto one of the earliest urban colonial populations in Nouvelle France, but previous bioarchaeological studies have produced conflicting interpretations regarding the presence of non-European or admixed individuals. Here, we generated ancient DNA from 45 individuals and applied genotype imputation, runs-of-homozygosity, and identity-by-descent analyses to reevaluate genetic relatedness and cemetery organization. Our results show exclusively French European ancestry. We observe low levels of close-kin unions and identify several genetic lineages distributed across the cemetery’s successive burial phases rather than family clustering or religious ordering. The spatial organization of the graves is consistent with rapid demographic growth, with successive burials overlapping one another, before being disrupted by urban development. Rooted in Indigenous decolonial frameworks, these findings challenge the ‘admixed founding population’ narrative, aligning with…

items.title: Chronic cigarette smoke exposure induces distinct stem cell states driving genetic driver–specific non–small cell lung cancer subtypes
items.summary_raw: Cigarette smoke-induced chronic inflammation (CI) potentiates development of non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) by mediating genetic and epigenetic events. Using normal lung organoids (LOs), we define how chronic cigarette smoke condensate (CSC) exposure drives two separate stem cell populations to evolve premalignant states harboring progressive epigenetic and linked transcriptomic abnormalities in the absence of major driver mutations. These dynamics facilitate evolution of an immune evasive state with downregulation of inflammatory pathways and accompanying death signals mediated by epigenetic silencing of PANoptosis regulator, Zbp1. The stem cell populations evolve through distinct trajectories to respond differently to subsequent introduction of oncogenic mutations, Kras G12V and loss of Tp53, to induce one step transformation of CSC exposed organoids resulting in two major NSCLC subtypes. Kras mutations drive tumorigenesis primarily in a bronchioalveolar stem cell–derived state producing adenocarcinomas while TP53 loss drives tumorigenesis in a basal stem cell–derived state resulting in squamous cell carcinomas. CSC-induced downregulation of Zbp1 and interferon signaling is further potentiated in tumors with mutation-specific changes marked by decreased expression in Kras-mutant contexts. Our findings define unique transcriptomic profiles in CI-induced stem cell states and reveal a key role for cell death pathway-associated genes in potentiating oncogenic drivers to…

Brain weight across the adult lifespan in great apes
items.summary_raw: Reduction in brain weight is a hallmark feature of human aging, which is exacerbated in pathologies, such as Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias. However, it remains unclear whether a decrease in brain weight with age reflects a vulnerability unique to the human lineage or represents a consequence of an extension of aging processes shared with other primates. To address this question, we examined age-related changes in brain weight across our closest living relatives, the great apes (chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas, and orangutans). The sample spanned the full adult age range in each species and included individuals reaching ages comparable to those at which age-related brain changes become apparent in humans. Across species, brain weight did not show significant change throughout adulthood and into advanced age. The observed pattern held even when body weight was included in the analysis in a subsample of chimpanzees. Overall, these results indicate that marked brain weight loss is not a general feature of great ape aging and instead appears largely specific to humans, with implications for understanding susceptibility to late-life brain pathology.

items.title: Formation of a swelling gel underlies a morphological transition in Bacillus subtilis biofilms
items.summary_raw: Microbes across diverse species and environments form biofilms, living materials composed of cells and extracellular polymers. Biofilm-dwelling cells benefit from emergent soft matter physics, which sculpts three-dimensional morphologies and facilitates osmotic nutrient uptake. Although biofilms are modeled as viscoelastic gels, the physical origins of the phase transition underlying their conversion from groups of cells to living gels have not been systematically investigated. Here, we show that Bacillus subtilis biofilms use polymer composition to tune their physical properties and drive gel formation. Using imaging, water immersion experiments, and rheological measurements with matrix knockout strains, we demonstrate the complementary roles of two polymers in this developmental transition: hydrophilic poly- γ -glutamic acid swells colonies by absorbing water while exopolysaccharides serve as effective cross-linkers, causing a sol–gel-like phase transition that imparts structural integrity. With matrix knockout coculture biofilms, we independently modulate the production of each polymer and reveal a phase space of biofilm morphologies. Colonies that produce both polymers develop macroscopic wrinkles. A thin-film model predicts biofilm wrinkling from swelling-induced internal strain coupled with elasticity. The model reproduces the shape of our observed morphological phase diagram. Our results demonstrate that bacteria leverage gelation to vary their material properties and…

items.title: Extended fractional Hofstadter states at high field in twisted bilayer graphene above the magic angle
items.summary_raw: When a Chern band is partially filled, a fractional Chern insulator (FCI)—the lattice analog of a fractional quantum Hall state—can arise. Though the full range of possible scenarios for producing such a state is not established, the most tractable models combine strong electronic interactions with the quantum geometry of the parent Chern band meeting specific criteria. In twisted bilayer graphene, the importance of interactions can be tuned by varying the interlayer twist. Here, we study a sample with twist near 1.4 ° , large enough to suppress the zero-field correlated states. We find that applying a strong magnetic field restores the importance of electron–electron interactions: at nearly half a magnetic flux quantum per moiré unit cell, deep in the Hofstadter regime, odd-denominator fractional states appear in multiple Hofstadter subbands. These fractional states persist over larger ranges of density, and are more robustly quantized, than nearby integer states, opposite to what is seen in other fractional quantum Hall and FCI systems.

The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure can fail to control the FDR for correlated two-sided Gaussian tests
items.summary_raw: The Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) procedure is the standard method for controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) in large-scale studies involving testing multiple hypotheses. Whether the BH procedure controls the FDR for every correlation structure among two-sided Gaussian tests has been a long-standing question, and a positive answer has been believed. Here, we settle the question negatively, by providing examples of Gaussian factor models for which the BH method fails to control the FDR at the nominal level. We prove mathematically that the violation holds, and also provide simulation results which are consistent with the theory. The level of violation can be characterized as mild but nonnegligible. In one of our examples, empirical FDR levels of ≈0.0106 and ≈0.053 are achieved for nominal FDR levels 0.01 and 0.05, respectively. Larger violations are also possible. The violation appears most prominently for large numbers (thousands) of tests; though we also present an example with a moderate number of 85 tests. We also briefly discuss the implications of our findings.

The more you automate, the less you see: Hidden pitfalls of autonomous AI scientists
items.summary_raw: The rapid rise of autonomous AI scientists marks a paradigm shift in scientific discovery by automating the research lifecycle. Yet their rushed development has outpaced critical oversight, leaving key workflow decisions dangerously unscrutinized. We present a much-needed systematic analysis of open-source AI scientist systems, investigating four primary pitfalls: inappropriate benchmark selection, data leakage, metric misuse, and post hoc selection bias. Through controlled experiments that isolate each pitfall, we find systematic vulnerabilities across two representative open-source systems. Crucially, we find that these flaws are largely invisible at the level of the final manuscript, suggesting that current manuscript-centric peer review paradigms are fundamentally insufficient for ensuring the integrity of automated research. We further propose mitigation strategies and demonstrate that access to full workflow artifacts (log traces and code) enables more effective auditing. Our findings suggest that journals, conferences, and researchers should move beyond manuscript-only evaluation toward process auditing the end-to-end workflow artifacts of AI scientist systems.

items.title: Tyrosine phosphorylation unfolds nucleophosmin and disrupts its integration into the nucleolus
items.summary_raw: Nucleophosmin (NPM1) is a multifunctional nucleolar protein essential for ribosome biogenesis, genome stability, and stress responses. Its integration into the nucleolus depends on its oligomerization and multivalent interactions that enable liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS). Here, we investigate how tyrosine phosphorylation at Tyr17, Tyr29, and Tyr67 located within the interface between monomers at the N-terminal oligomerization domain regulates NPM1 structure and function. Replacing tyrosines with p- carboxymethyl-L-phenylalanine as phosphomimetic substitutions, we show that phosphorylation at Tyr17 and Tyr67 disrupts key intermonomer interactions and destabilizes the NPM1 pentameric assembly, which drives an order-to-disorder transition and impairs binding to nuclear partners. Consequently, dual phosphorylation at Tyr17 and Tyr67 disturbs both homotypic and heterotypic LLPS, thereby impairing incorporation of NPM1 into the nucleolus. This altered localization of NPM1 serves as a hallmark of p53 activation, driven both by nucleoplasmic NPM1 and by the release of ARF from NPM1-dependent sequestration in the nucleolus. Altogether, our results provide a molecular mechanistic explanation on how phosphorylation-induced structural and dynamic changes drive the release of NPM1 from the nucleolus under genotoxic stress.

items.title: Regulation of morphogen signaling pathways by recurrent hypermotif circuits
items.summary_raw: Morphogen signaling pathways orchestrate cell fate and tissue patterning during embryo development through intricate intercellular communication. While much is known about the molecular components of these pathways, the underlying regulatory logic shaping their integration remains unclear. Here, we develop a computational framework to uncover higher-order network structures, hypermotifs , that link gene regulatory circuits within and between cells via morphogen signaling. Applying this framework to single-cell RNA sequencing data from human intestinal development, we identify recurrent hypermotif topologies that mediate communication between epithelial and fibroblast populations. These cell-cell hypermotif circuits involve feedback and feedforward loops embedded within signaling pathways. Dynamical modeling reveals that such circuits can generate emergent behaviors, including oscillatory and antagonistic responses. Our results highlight hypermotifs as key design principles in developmental regulatory networks, providing a systems-level understanding of morphogen signal integration across cell types.

A 2,623-year temperature reconstruction from the Colorado Rocky Mountains reveals warm and cool droughts
items.summary_raw: Recent hydrological drought in the US Southwest has occurred under exceptional warming, intensifying water deficits in the Colorado River and Rio Grande basins. Yet the long-term role of temperature in modulating severe and persistent droughts remains poorly understood because regional temperature reconstructions are scarce. We present a 2,623-y June–September minimum temperature reconstruction from the southern Colorado Rocky Mountains based on Pinus aristata tree rings, spanning 600 BCE to 2022 CE. The reconstruction reveals decadal-to-multidecadal variability but limited expression of sustained hemispheric climate phases. In contrast, late 20th and early 21st century warming is unprecedented in magnitude, persistence, and spatial coherence across western North America. By pairing this reconstruction with a continuous 2,000-y reconstruction of upper Colorado River streamflow, we evaluate temperature conditions during major droughts. The most severe and persistent drought of the Common Era, during the 2nd century CE, developed under a persistent cool anomaly, indicating that extreme hydrologic deficit can arise from precipitation forcing alone. Over the last two millennia, warm droughts were more frequent than cool droughts (56% vs. 44%), but both produced comparable cumulative flow deficits. In contrast to the conventional characterization of droughts as hot and dry, these findings demonstrate that extreme droughts developed under both cool and warm regimes and suggest…

items.summary_raw: Proper development of the inner ear, including specification and differentiation of progenitors for the endolymphatic sac, is crucial for hearing and balance. In a mouse model of the SOX9 Y440X/+ mutation that causes campomelic dysplasia and deafness, impaired development of the endolymphatic system at mid-gestation was associated with SOX10 downregulation. The underlying molecular causes and significance are unclear. Here, we found in Sox9 Y440X/+ mice, Sox10 expression was downregulated, prior to overt differentiation, in the dorsomedial aspect of the E10.5 otic vesicle that normally becomes the endolymphatic duct and sac. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling of E10.5 otic vesicles showed increased expression of Wnt pathway genes that was associated with the domain-specific decrease in Sox10 expression. Forced elevation of Wnt signaling by expression of stabilized β-catenin in the early otocyst and more developed inner ears, suppressed Sox10 expression. Wnt exerted an inhibitory effect on SOX10 expression in otocyst-like organoids derived from human pluripotent stem cells. In vitro transactivation assays reveal antagonistic action of SOX9 and Wnt signaling on Sox10 transactivation mediated by conserved enhancers with neighboring/overlapping SOX9- and TCF/LEF-binding (Wnt effectors) motifs. We propose a conserved SOX9-Wnt antagonism acting via conserved enhancers, regulates SOX10 to modulate endolymphatic cell fate. The SOX9 Y440X/+ mutation disrupts this regulatory circuit…

items.title: Recurrent hypermotif regulatory circuits in developmental programs
items.summary_raw: During development, cells self-organize into complex spatial and temporal patterns driven by regulatory circuits of transcription factors and morphogen signaling. However, the principles that govern these regulatory interactions remain poorly understood. Here, we introduce a framework to dissect the building-block circuits of developmental gene regulatory networks and explore their integration into higher-order hypermotif circuits. Using single-cell RNA-sequencing data spanning human intestinal development, we identify five recurrent network motifs, including feedforward and feedback loops, and investigate their roles in the regulation of gene expression. Our analysis reveals distinct categories of developmental genes based on their roles within network motifs, highlighting major transitions in regulatory architecture across developmental stages. Furthermore, we model the emergent dynamical properties of hypermotif circuits, including their potential roles in regulating morphogen signaling. This study uncovers a common theme in regulatory circuits of developmental programs, emphasizing how the combinatorial wiring of regulatory motifs enables robust and diverse tissue formation.

items.title: Apomixis imposes evolutionary costs by reducing recombination efficiency and disrupting segregation
items.summary_raw: Sexual reproduction facilitates the purging of deleterious mutations via recombination. Apomixis, defined by asexual seed formation, involves suppressed meiosis, thereby reducing the efficacy of purifying selection. However, the evolutionary consequences of apomixis remain poorly understood. In this study, we used wild citrus ( Citrus hindsii ), which has both sexual and apomictic (adventitious embryony) lineages, as a diploid genetic system (2n = 2x = 18). We performed a cross between a sexual and an apomictic individual (pollen donor), generated haplotype-resolved genome assemblies for the two parents, and deep-sequenced 226 progeny. These data were integrated into a graph pangenome to characterize the meiotic recombination landscape. The apomictic lineage harbors 1.28-fold more heterozygous structural variations, which may locally suppress crossovers. Furthermore, apomictic recombination efficiency is reduced by 24.2% relative to the sexual lineage. Crucially, the contribution of male function through outcrossing exposes a substantial recessive genetic load, including a putative gamete-lethal mutation, triggering significant segregation distortion across 31.7% of the genome. We established that these distortion profiles are driven by the cumulative effects of multiple loci, with the magnitude of distortion depending on haplotype interactions. Collectively, our study quantifies the recombination landscape of apomixis and provides a framework for unmasking and mitigating…

Causality-integrated graph learning for multi-endpoint toxicity prediction
items.summary_raw: Toxicity prediction remains a longstanding challenge in the safety assessment of numerous artificial chemicals. While conventional single-endpoint models are effective for predicting many molecular properties, they fail to capture the complex mechanisms underlying toxicity, which involve multiple molecular targets, interconnected pathways, and diverse outcomes. We present a causality-integrated graph learning framework that embeds toxicological mechanisms extracted from large-scale literature mining as directed graphs within deep learning (DL) models. By using chemical structure as input, the framework generates compound-specific perturbation profiles within a fixed causal space, enabling system-level classification, quantitative prioritization, and mechanistic interpretation across multiple outcomes. Focusing on endocrine-disrupting chemicals, we constructed a large-scale, causally organized knowledge graph (EDKG) and implemented the framework as EDKG-DL, a predictive model that incorporates mechanism-aware graph reasoning. Through extensive external validations, EDKG-DL outperforms structure-driven state-of-the-art approaches in both stability and cross-scenario generalization. This work establishes a mechanism-constrained, causality-informed learning paradigm that is highly relevant for multi-endpoint toxicity assessment and regulatory decision-making.

items.title: Global divergence in urban–rural vegetation resilience driven by broken ecological trade-offs
items.summary_raw: While urban environments are known to extend growing seasons and enhance vegetation growth, whether these benefits also improve resilience to climate stress or instead create productive but vulnerable ecosystems remains uncertain. Using satellite observations from 2001 to 2022 across 751 large cities in 109 countries, we find that urban vegetation is more resilient than surrounding rural vegetation in 78% of cities. This urban–rural resilience gap has widened over time, driven by declining rural resilience alongside slightly improving urban recovery dynamics, particularly in arid regions where rural vegetation shows progressively slower recovery. Among the factors examined, the urban irrigation proxy, quantified as the urban–rural difference in evapotranspiration, was the strongest correlate of the urban resilience advantage, followed by canopy structure. In 32% of cities, predominantly located in arid regions, urban vegetation exhibited a dual advantage, combining smaller disturbance-related greenness losses with faster recovery than rural vegetation, consistent with management-mediated relaxation of the resistance–resilience trade-off. These findings challenge the view of cities as uniformly detrimental to ecosystem stability and suggest that, when supported by sustainable and equitable management, urban green spaces may serve as managed refugia for vegetation resilience under climate change.

An unidentified reservoir of comet 81P/Wild 2 chondrules
items.summary_raw: Comets, which have been stored in the cryogenic regions for billions of years, preserve key records of the solar system’s formation and the dynamic evolution of planets and other small bodies. Twenty years ago, NASA Stardust mission returned samples from a Jupiter-family comet, 81P/Wild 2, for laboratory analysis, and uncovered an unexpected truth that this comet is not entirely made of interstellar grains but contains significant amounts of high-temperature silicate fragments. However, the sources of these fragments remain ambiguous. Here, we report the petrography and oxygen three-isotopes of ~100 silicate fragments from track 227, one of the largest impact tracks in the Stardust aerogel collector. The fragments are mostly pieces of small chondrules (typically <60 µm) with many exhibiting igneous textures such as microporphyritic olivine and, occasionally, nonporphyritic barred olivine and cryptocrystalline. Approximately 90% of the fragments define a modest negative correlation between the mass-independent fractionation of oxygen isotopes (Δ 17 O = δ 17 O –0.52 × δ 18 O, –4 to 0‰) and the redox state [Mg# = mol% Mg/(Mg + Fe), 100 to 62]. The remaining 10% are markedly FeO-rich (Mg# <60) and 16 O-depleted (Δ 17 O up to 7‰). These characteristics distinguish them from chondrules in any known chondrite groups, nor can they be reproduced by mixing chondrule populations in any proportion. Instead, these fragments are from an unidentified chondrule reservoir in a more distant…

items.title: The Booming Market for DIY Fire Protection
items.summary_raw: Nicholai Allen, a Southern California wildland firefighter, opened his Instagram DMs this summer to find a photo of a beautiful A-frame home set against a backdrop of mountains and pine forests. At first glance, it looked almost like an advertisement for a vacation rental. But the amazing thing about the picture was not the cozy mountain scene, but the fact that the house was still standing. “Very thankful this product works,” read the accompanying text. “Saved our house and all our outbuildings. Little Giant Fire.” Allen is a firefighter — he was on the scene when the Pacific Palisades burned in 2025 — and a wildfire survivor, having evacuated his family from the deadly Woolsey Fire near Malibu in 2018. He’s also the founder of Safe Soss, a home-hardening company advertising a “three-step supplemental wildfire defense system,” which includes a carbon filter ember guard, ember tape, and the company’s marquee product: an ammonium phosphate-based wildfire risk-reduction spray. They’re all sold at Lowe’s, where you can get the whole kit for less than $200. “In the aftermath [of the Woolsey fire], I kept asking: How come some homes survived, and some didn’t?” Allen recounted to me. “Some get retardant dropped on them, and some don’t. items.title: Extreme heat left this student athlete on life support. He won’t be the last.
items.summary_raw: Matthew Mayich stepped onto the field of Sun Angel Stadium in Tempe, Arizona, at about 7 a.m. on August 20. It was the standout hockey player’s first official practice with his new team, and temperatures were already in the mid-80s. He and his Arizona State University teammates spent at least 45 minutes doing push-ups , planks, flutter kicks, bear crawls, squats, sprints, and buddy-carries, led by guest trainer and former Green Beret Tim Ziesel. Before leaving the field, Ziesel gave instructions for one final exercise: a medicine ball run. As temperatures approached 90 degrees Fahrenheit, the players set off in small groups, according to the university’s timeline of events . Mayich appeared to struggle, then stumbled, dropped the ball, and fell. He tried to rise and fell again. Athletic staff treated him with iced towels and cool water, then sprayed him with a garden hose. Initially responsive, his condition deteriorated, and the trainer called 911. Paramedics rushed him to the hospital, where he remains in critical condition after experiencing what his family’s lawyer, Robert Carey, called exertional heat stroke. Carey did not respond to requests for additional information about the diagnosis, which could not be independently corroborated. He has told journalists the family’s hope for a meaningful recovery hovers near a miracle . “We want accountability for what happened to our son,” Mayich’s parents, John and Christina, said in a written statement. “We want the truth.”…

items.title: Food and climate change in the media: a case study of the international coverage of the Dubai COP in 2023
items.summary_raw: Abstract The UN’s annual climate change negotiations, known as the Conference of Parties (COPs), are crucial venues for raising awareness and advancing international dialogue on climate challenges. Mainstream media play a key role in shaping how the public and policymakers understand them. At COP28 in Dubai (2023), food systems - responsible for 21%-37% of total global greenhouse gas emissions – received unprecedented attention, despite their traditional neglect in the climate discourse. This study used manual content analysis to assess how around 50 news outlets across five countries where the agricultural export or food sector are particularly important to their economies (Argentina, Australia, Brazil, the UK, and the USA) covered the link between food, diet, and climate change during COP28. We find that media coverage of the food-climate nexus remained limited, as only 6% of all COP28 coverage discussed food in depth. Actors defending the meat and livestock sector – mainly trade groups and politicians – were as prominent as those calling for food system reform, such as NGOs and international agencies. The most common pro-reform argument emphasized the climate impact of food systems, while defenders of meat production highlighted environmental benefits, food security, and nutrition. Few articles mentioned the prominent presence of food industry lobbyists at the conference. Our findings suggest the need for further research into the obstacles to more frequent, thorough and…

items.title: Two years after Hurricane Helene, survivors are taking lessons for the future
items.summary_raw: In the days and weeks after Hurricane Helene, people throughout western North Carolina and beyond found themselves thrust into new situations, forced to learn new skills to help themselves and their neighbors. Community centers, churches, and fire departments flung open their doors, and for months, they buzzed with activity. Stacks of clothes covered altars. Tools and equipment filled spare rooms. Residents learned how to strip homes to the studs and built networks for bringing food, water, and other essential supplies to one another. Now, two years later, people want to turn these ad hoc efforts — which supported communities through the loss of power, water, internet, and other crucial services — into more permanent fixtures of local disaster response, called “resilience hubs.” “It’s become one of those terms, I think, that sometimes feels a little nebulous to people,” McKenzie Jones, a director with Urban Sustainability Directors Network, said. “But resilience hubs are just existing community spaces that are used and trusted by residents.” The East Asheville Library, for instance, is installing solar panels. At the Asheville Tool Library, people are learning how to wield power tools. And at the Old Fort Train Depot, locals recently discussed a heat wave action plan during an ice cream social. The city is stepping up as well. Earlier this year, Asheville set aside $2 million to shore up the city’s existing hubs. City Manager D.K. Wesley made a soft commitment of spending up…
